A.explanation: This is $mh/t$ without $g$, giving about $600 \text{ W}$. Weight is $mg$, not $m$, so gravitational potential energy must include $g$.

B.explanation: Useful work $mgh$ divided by $3600 \text{ s}$ gives about $5900 \text{ W}$, which is $5.9 \text{ kW}$.

C.explanation: This is about six times too large and follows from using too short a time, such as $600 \text{ s}$ instead of $1.0$ hour $= 3600 \text{ s}$.

D.explanation: This is about sixty times too large and follows from dividing the energy by $60 \text{ s}$ instead of $3600 \text{ s}$ for $1.0$ hour.

hints: Notice the pump raises $27 \times 10^3 \text{ kg}$ through $80 \text{ m}$, so the useful energy transferred is gravitational potential energy $mgh$.
Recall average power is useful energy divided by time, $P = mgh/t$, with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Convert the $1.0$ hour time to $3600 \text{ s}$ before dividing, then convert the answer in $\text{W}$ to $\text{kW}$ to compare with the options.
walkthrough: Identify the useful energy: raising water at steady rate increases gravitational potential energy by $\Delta E_p = mgh$, with $m = 27 \times 10^3 \text{ kg}$ and $h = 80 \text{ m}$.
State the power rule: average useful output power is $P = \Delta E_p/t = mgh/t$.
Convert time to SI units: $t = 1.0 \text{ hour} = 60 \times 60 \text{ s} = 3600 \text{ s}$.
Substitute values with units: $P = (27 \times 10^3 \text{ kg})(9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2})(80 \text{ m})/(3600 \text{ s})$.
Calculate the energy first: $(27 \times 10^3)(9.81)(80) \approx 2.12 \times 10^7 \text{ J}$, then divide by time: $2.12 \times 10^7/3600 \approx 5890 \text{ W} \approx 5.9 \text{ kW}$.
